title: Turkish Airlines 301
summary: Turkish Airlines Flight 301, a Fokker F28-1000, crashed during takeoff at Izmir Airport on 26 January 1974. The aircraft had spent the night outside in freezing temperatures, and frost accumulated on the wings which was unnoticed by the crew. During takeoff, the pilots over-rotated the aircraft, causing it to stall. The stalled aircraft climbed only 8-10 meters before pitching down and veering left, crashing into the ground and catching fire. All 67 of the 73 occupants were killed.
probable_cause: Aircraft stalled on takeoff due to over-rotation and frost accretion on the wings. Calculations showed the aircraft would have reached takeoff speed after 2,800 feet of runway but actually rotated after 3,200 feet at a speed of 124 knots.

title: Pan Am 806
summary: Pan Am Flight 806 departed Auckland on 30 January 1974 with 91 passengers and 10 crew for a flight to Los Angeles with stops at Pago Pago and Honolulu. On approach to Pago Pago, the aircraft encountered microburst wind shear. At 23:40:42, the 707 came into contact with trees 3865 ft short of runway 5 threshold while descending through weather. The aircraft impacted the ground 236 feet further and plowed through dense vegetation for another 539 ft before crashing into a three-foot high rock wall. All four engines were torn from the wings and a post-impact fire consumed most of the aircraft, killing 97 persons. Four crew and passengers initially survived but died later.
probable_cause: The flight crew's tardy identification of microburst-induced wind shear. Other factors included poor visibility, lack of altitude and airspeed callouts by the aircrew.

title: Turkish Airlines 981
summary: Turkish Airlines Flight 981, a DC-10 flying Istanbul to London via Paris, crashed into the Ermenonville Forest outside Paris on 3 March 1974 after its rear cargo door blew off during the climb from Orly, killing all 346 aboard. The explosive decompression tore a section of cabin floor and six occupied seats out through the open hatch, severing the control cables that ran beneath it and destroying the crew's ability to control the elevators, rudder and number two engine. Investigators found the door's locking pins had been filed down and a required handle support plate had never been fitted.
probable_cause: The crash was caused by an incorrectly secured, defectively designed rear cargo door that blew open in flight, causing explosive decompression that collapsed the cabin floor and severed the control cables to the elevators, rudder and number two engine.

factors.evidence: The rear left cargo door blew off after the aircraft passed Meaux, and the pressure difference forced the cabin floor through the open hatch.
The linkage between the door handle and the locking pins was too weak, letting the handle close with the latches in the wrong position.
Ground crews had filed the cargo door's locking pins down to less than a quarter of an inch.
The pressure differential forced six occupied passenger seats to be ejected through the open hatch.
The primary and backup control cables beneath the collapsed floor were severed, destroying control of the elevators, rudder and number two engine.
The throttle for engine two snapped shut and the aircraft immediately pitched into a steep nose-down attitude.

title: Sterling Airways 901
summary: Sterling Airways Flight 901, a Sud Aviation Caravelle chartered by tour company with 96 aboard, experienced landing gear failure while taxiing for takeoff at Tehran. The right main landing gear collapsed due to structural failure, causing right wing to contact runway and rupture a fuel tank. Spilled fuel ignited, resulting in fire that killed 15 passengers and injured 37 others.

title: Pan Am 812
summary: Pan Am Flight 812, a Boeing 707, crashed into a mountain near Denpasar, Bali on April 22, 1974 while preparing for approach to Ngurah Rai Airport. Multiple eyewitnesses reported the aircraft was on fire before striking Mesehe Mountain, and the crew appears to have attempted approach from the northwest where terrain was steeper rather than the standard eastern approach.
probable_cause: The aircraft struck a mountain during approach to Denpasar. Investigation concluded the aircraft did not break up in flight, engines were functioning properly, and the aircraft was airworthy. The crew's attempt to approach from the northwest into mountainous terrain was the primary factor.

title: 1974 Leningrad Aeroflot Il-18 crash
summary: An Aeroflot Ilyushin Il-18 carrying 102 passengers and 7 crew departed Leningrad for Krasnodar on April 27, 1974. Minutes after takeoff, the number 4 engine caught fire. The crew declared an emergency and attempted to return to Pulkovo Airport. After completing four approach maneuvers, as the aircraft reduced speed to land, the fire gained intensity and destroyed the right wing's mechanical functions. The aircraft rolled abruptly to the right and crashed near railroad tracks 1.5 km from the airport, killing all 109 aboard.
probable_cause: Fire in the number 4 engine destroyed the aircraft's mechanical control systems during the approach phase.

title: TWA 841 (1974)

summary: TWA Flight 841, a Boeing 707, departed Tel Aviv for New York via Athens and Rome on September 8, 1974, carrying 79 passengers and 9 crew members. About 30 minutes after takeoff from Rome, the aircraft crashed into the Ionian Sea approximately 50 nautical miles west of Cephalonia, Greece. The National Transportation Safety Board determined that a bomb hidden in the cargo hold had destroyed the aircraft. The bomb detonated systems responsible for operating the plane's control surfaces, causing the aircraft to pitch up steeply, stall, and enter a death spiral into the sea.

title: Eastern Air Lines 212
summary: Eastern Air Lines Flight 212 crashed near Charlotte while approaching the airport from Charleston. The flight crew was engrossed in idle conversation instead of monitoring their flight instruments and altitude during the critical descent phase. The aircraft descended far below the safe altitude and crashed several miles before the runway. The probable cause was pilot error and lack of altitude awareness, leading to the establishment of the sterile cockpit rule.
probable_cause: The flight crew's lack of altitude awareness and poor cockpit discipline during the approach, with nonessential discussion distracting pilots from their flying duties. The crew's persistent attempt to visually identify the Carolina Skytower further distracted and confused them.

The aircraft then lost control, plunged to the ground from 1000 feet, killing all 75 people aboard.

title: Lufthansa 540
summary: Lufthansa Flight 540, a Boeing 747-130, crashed shortly after taking off from Embakasi Airport in Nairobi on November 20, 1974. Almost immediately after liftoff, the crew felt buffeting vibration. The leading-edge slats were left in the retracted position due to the flight engineer failing to open the slat system bleed air valves as required on the pre-flight checklist. The aircraft was unable to climb out of ground effect and started to descend while the stall warning light activated. The aircraft crashed into grass 3,700 feet from the end of the runway, struck an elevated access road, and broke apart. Of the 139 passengers and 18 crew members on board, 54 passengers and 5 crew members were killed.
probable_cause: The flight engineer failed to open the slat system bleed air valve on the pre-flight checklist, preventing the pneumatic slat system from deploying the leading-edge slats for takeoff. The crew failed to recognize the warning lights indicating this condition, and the takeoff warning system did not have a separate alert for the slat valve status. The failure to deploy slats resulted in an excessive stall speed and the inability to maintain flight, leading to controlled flight into terrain.

The faulty state of the slats should have been indicated by yellow warning lights, but the crew reported the lights appeared green; the takeoff warning system did not have a separate warning for the slat valve.
The crew failed to perform a satisfactory pre-takeoff checklist to verify the slat valve had been opened.
The takeoff warning system which would have warned of flap positioning did not include a separate warning that the slats' pneumatic valve had not been opened by the flight engineer.
Without the slats being extended, the aircraft's stall speed was higher and the maximum angle of attack was lower, preventing the aircraft from climbing out of ground effect.
The aircraft crashed into grass 3,700 feet from the end of the runway, then struck an elevated access road and broke up.

title: TWA 514
summary: TWA Flight 514 was diverted to Washington Dulles due to severe weather with high crosswinds on the original approach. During vectoring for a non-precision approach to runway 12, the crew descended to 1800 ft shown on the first checkpoint but became confused about whether they were still on a radar-controlled segment that allowed safe descent. At 11:09:22 a.m. EST, the Boeing 727 impacted the west slope of Mount Weather at 1670 ft above sea level at 230 knots, killing all 92 occupants.

title: Northwest Airlines 6231
summary: Northwest Airlines Flight 6231, a Boeing 727, crashed in Harriman State Park near Stony Point, New York after experiencing a stall and rapid descent caused by pitot probe blockage from atmospheric icing. As the aircraft climbed past 16,000 feet, the overspeed warning horn sounded followed by a stick shaker stall warning. The crew's improper reaction to erroneous airspeed readings caused the aircraft to stall. The aircraft descended from 24,000 feet to ground level in 83 seconds, with the horizontal stabilizer separating from high G-forces.
probable_cause: Loss of control resulted from the flight crew failing to recognize and correct the aircraft's high angle of attack, low-speed stall and descending spiral. The stall was precipitated by the crew's improper reaction to erroneous airspeed and Mach indications which had resulted from blockage of the pitot heads by atmospheric icing. The pitot head heaters had not been activated.

The flight crew pulled back on the control column, which caused the aircraft to stall.
The aircraft went into a low-speed stall at high angle of attack.
The aircraft started to descend out of control in a right-hand spin, reaching vertical acceleration of plus 5g due to tight nosedow spiral with bank angle between 70 and 80 degrees.
At about 3500 feet, a large portion of the aircraft's horizontal stabilizer separated due to the high G-forces.
